tasks.title: Read the announcement on a thread of its own
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1`, write a class `Announcer` with one method. `static Thread announce(List<String> lines, Speaker speaker)` makes a new thread that hands each line to `speaker.say`, in order, starts it, and gives that thread back at once, without waiting for the lines to be said. `Speaker` is given above the tasks.

Check hands `announce` lines of its own and a speaker of its own. Its speaker holds each line it is given on another thread until `announce` has returned, so Check sees whether the lines were said on a thread of their own, by the very thread given back, in order, and whether `announce` came back before they were said.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson about making a thread.
Make the Thread with a lambda that says the lines, one after another.
Start it, then give it back.
Take the // off the first group of lines in main and run it: the hut line comes before the speaker's.
hints: A Thread is made with the work it is to do, as a lambda with no parameters: the same shape of lambda as the Runnable in the lesson.
Making a Thread runs nothing. One method gives it a life of its own; another, with a name that looks right, runs the work on the thread that calls it, like any method.
`Thread reader = new Thread(() -> { for (String line : lines) speaker.say(line); });`, then `reader.start();` and `return reader;`.

tasks.title: Count every boat's list at once
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a class `Counting` with one method, with `throws InterruptedException`. `static int total(List<Manifest> manifests)` starts one thread for each manifest, all of them before it waits for any. Each thread calls `count()` on its manifest once. Give each thread a place of its own for its answer, such as its own place in an array: threads adding into one shared total can lose a count, as the next issue shows. Then `total` waits for every thread to end and gives back the counts added up. `Manifest` is given above the tasks.

Check hands `total` manifests of its own. Their `count()` holds every thread until `total` is waiting for its threads, and Check counts at that moment how many threads had been started, then lets the counts through one at a time. It reads what `total` gives back, how many times each manifest was counted and on which thread. Once more it interrupts the thread that called `total` while it waits, and sees whether the `InterruptedException` reaches it.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson about join and about InterruptedException.
Make an array with a place for each manifest, and a list for the threads.
In one loop, start a thread per manifest that puts its count in its place.
In a second loop, wait for each thread; then add up the array.
hints: Two loops: one that starts the threads, and one that waits for them. A wait inside the first loop holds up the next start.
A lambda can use a local variable only when it never changes, so the loop's own counter cannot go in; a copy made inside the loop can. A thread that has ended has finished writing its place.
`int at = i; Thread t = new Thread(() -> counts[at] = manifests.get(at).count()); t.start(); threads.add(t);` in the first loop, `for (Thread t : threads) t.join();` after it, then add up `counts`.

tasks.title: Ring the quay bell until the hut closes
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a class `Ringer` with two methods. `static Thread start(Bell bell, long everyMillis)` starts a thread that rings the bell, sleeps `everyMillis` milliseconds with `Thread.sleep`, and does it again, until the thread is interrupted, and gives the thread back at once. Interrupted while it sleeps or while it rings, the thread ends. `static void stop(Thread ringer)`, with `throws InterruptedException`, interrupts the thread and waits for it to end. `Bell` is given above the tasks.

Check starts a ringer on a bell of its own three times: once it stops it while the ringer is ringing (its bell holds that ring until `stop` is waiting or has returned), once while the ringer is asleep, and once after a few rings. It counts the rings after `stop` was called, sees whether `stop` returned while the ringer was still ringing, and whether the ringer ended.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson about interrupting a thread.
Write start: a thread whose loop rings and sleeps, and a catch that ends it when it is interrupted.
Write stop: ask the ringer to stop, then wait for it.
Take the // off the last group of lines in main and run it: the bell rings, then the hut closes and the program ends.
hints: The lesson's interrupt part has all of it: what a sleeping thread does when it is interrupted, and what a catch must not do with it.

Where the catch sits decides what an interrupt does: a catch outside the loop ends the loop; an empty one inside it carries on as if nothing had happened. stop does two things, in an order: ask, then wait.

In start: `new Thread(() -> { try { while (true) { bell.ring(); Thread.sleep(everyMillis); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { /* the hut is closing: end here */ } })`, started and given back. In stop: `ringer.interrupt(); ringer.join();`.
